saturation_history.rationale: Not tested: the taxonomy was generated from this minibatch.

Most open codes are covered by existing dimensions: availability and dashboard updates fit Real-Time Status Communication; payment adapters, a common interface, facade, and provider delegation fit Payment Integration Modularity; secure credential transmission and storage fit Data Protection Encryption Scope; rental-state notifications and Command-based rental operations fit the existing rental lifecycle and status-communication concerns. However, the taxonomy has no dimension for user authentication and account-verification architecture. Verification-code generation and delivery, verification-code expiration policy, and email-password authentication introduce relevant variation in identity verification and login mechanisms that cannot be absorbed without conflating them with encryption, payment, or rental lifecycle concerns. The explicitly rejected notification-scheduling code does not represent an adopted architectural concept and does not create a coverage gap.

Repository pattern for bike data and usage statistics
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers rental state-machine management, scheduled rental notifications, authentication and verification-code validity, and real-time status communication. Thus, the State-pattern lifecycle code, scheduled timing notifications, and both 30-second and 30-minute verification-code expiration codes are subsumed by existing dimensions, although the differing TTLs may indicate inconsistent source decisions rather than new dimensions. However, session lifecycle management—manual logout, inactivity termination, and its 15-minute threshold—is not captured by the existing authentication dimension, which focuses on authentication methods and verification credentials. Persistence and data-access abstraction for bike and usage data are also absent. Finally, usage-history report generation, downloadable reporting, and report-format variation are distinct from the existing real-time dashboard/status dimension and reveal an uncovered reporting/document-generation concern.

The taxonomy covers registration-data encryption, authentication, credential handling, notification dissemination, and proximity-based bike queries. However, it has no dimension for the architectural decision of which user data fields are collected during registration, including optional collection and data-minimization choices. Registration-data encryption does not subsume the collection policy itself. Thumbprint login is covered by Account Access and Session Security, but immediate deletion of biometric data after authentication introduces a distinct retention/deletion concern not captured by the encryption-scope dimension. The Observer notifications and bike-location proximity filtering are already covered by Bike Status Dissemination and Bike Tracking and Monitoring Architecture, respectively.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: No overlapping dimension questions are evident. The taxonomy distinguishes authentication methods (6), session termination (7), verification-code validity (14), privacy controls (10), bike-location architecture (4), payment-provider integration (9), and rental lifecycle management (1). Although some values concern related security or expiration topics, they answer different questions about authentication, session state, code lifetime, or data protection, so no merge or value move is required under this criterion.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions have understandable scopes and several values are concrete and distinguishable, especially 4 (Bike Location Service Architecture), 6 (Account Authentication Methods), and 14 (Verification Code Validity). The main weakness is overlap and mixed specificity in 10 (Data Protection and Privacy Controls): 10.3 overlaps with 10.1/10.2, while 10.4 and 10.5 are narrower restatements of those encryption values; consolidate or drop these redundant values. In 9 (Payment Integration Modularity), 9.1 (Modular payment behavior variation) is vague compared with the concrete adapter, interface, and facade values; rename it to the more specific “Strategy-based payment behavior variation” or drop it. In 7 (Session Termination Policies), 7.4 (Secure user access control) is a generic objective rather than a distinguishable termination policy; drop it, and incorporate 7.3’s fifteen-minute detail into 7.2 if it is intended as that policy’s parameter.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy represents several relevant decision areas with multiple candidates, notably Bike Location Service Architecture (4.1–4.2), Payment Integration Modularity (9.1–9.4), authentication, session management, rental lifecycle, and privacy controls. However, major areas explicitly required by the CityBike use case have no decision point: service decomposition, API gateway/request routing, service discovery, real-time communication patterns, observability/distributed tracing, and regulatory-compliance mechanisms for GDPR, the Privacy Directive, ISO 27001, and EU/China standards. Data Protection and Privacy Controls (10) addresses encryption and biometrics but does not provide alternatives for compliance mechanisms. Revise by reorganizing existing dimensions and values where possible, but the output currently contains no existing candidates that can represent these missing architectural concerns.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: All seven dimensions are within the CityBike use-case scope. Location architecture directly addresses real-time positioning and nearby-bike queries within 1000 meters; payment modularity addresses third-party payment integration; rental lifecycle covers QR unlocking and rental completion; authentication, session termination, verification-code validity, and data-protection controls address the required security, privacy, GDPR, and payment-data concerns. No dimension is unrelated or merely outside the stated subject, lifecycle, or architectural-decision scope.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: No dimension or value is an explicit catch-all bucket such as “Other,” “Miscellaneous,” or “General considerations.” The broad Data Protection and Privacy Controls dimension is still populated with specific encryption, credential, biometric, and deletion mechanisms, while the remaining dimensions target concrete concerns such as bike location, payment integration, authentication, sessions, and verification-code validity. No catch-all needs removal or reorganization.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Several entries are subtopics or details rather than alternatives to one decision. In dimension 7, value 7.3 (Fifteen-minute inactivity threshold) is a parameter of 7.2, and 7.4 (Secure user access control) is an objective/outcome rather than a candidate decision; remove them or reorganize 7.2 to contain the timeout policy without treating these as peer values. In dimension 4, 4.1 (Dedicated real-time location service) concerns service decomposition while 4.2 (Proximity-filtered bike location queries) concerns query behavior; separate the concerns using existing content or drop the orphaned subtopic. In dimension 10, 10.3, 10.4, and 10.5 are narrower scopes or applications of the broader encryption controls 10.1 and 10.2, and 10.7 is an objective rather than an alternative; fold the narrower values into the relevant encryption decisions and remove or reclassify the objective. Dimension 9 also lists implementation mechanisms (9.2 Adapter-based integration, 9.3 Common interface, and 9.4 Facade delegation) that can be parts of one modular integration approach rather than peer answers, so consolidate them under the broader modularity decision or drop the mechanism-level entries.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: Several dimensions have at least two values, but important groups do not represent one decision question. Dimension 10, Data Protection and Privacy Controls, mixes transport/storage encryption, credential handling, and biometric retention; split it into encryption controls (10.1–10.5) and biometric-data handling (10.6–10.7). Dimension 4 mixes a service architecture choice (4.1) with a query constraint (4.2); move 4.2 to an existing query/filter decision point or remove the orphan rather than treating it as an alternative. Dimension 1 combines state-transition management (1.1) with event-triggered automation (1.2), so merge these into an existing lifecycle question only if both remain alternatives, or move the odd value. Dimension 7 contains policy alternatives (7.1–7.2), a parameter of 7.2 (7.3), and a security objective rather than a decision (7.4); fold 7.3 into 7.2 and reclassify or remove 7.4. In dimension 4, values 4.2 "Bike status and usage data aggregation" and 4.3 "Real-time dashboard updates" are monitoring/dissemination subtopics; move them to dimension 3 or incorporate them into descriptions, while retaining 4.1 as the tracking approach. In dimension 8, value 8.3 "Independent payment behavior variation" is an outcome and 8.7 "Internal payment-provider delegation" is an implementation subtopic; drop them or fold them into the relevant adapter/facade value. In dimension 10, values 10.3 "Registration-data encryption," 10.4 "Secure transmission of login credentials," and 10.5 "Credential storage" are narrower scope subtopics; merge them into 10.1/10.2 descriptions or remove them. In dimension 11, values 11.2 "Downloadable usage-history reports" and 11.3 "Report-generation variation" describe outcomes/capabilities rather than choices; fold them into descriptions or drop them. Value 6.4 "Secure user access control" is likewise an outcome, so remove it or incorporate it into the authentication/session descriptions.

criteria.reason: The taxonomy has several serious structural violations. Dimensions 5 (Domain Event Automation) and 9 (Rental Pricing Variation) each contain only one candidate decision; merge their values into the relevant rental-behavior decision point, such as dimension 1, rather than retaining singleton dimensions. Dimension 4 mixes distinct questions—location-service architecture (4.1), data aggregation (4.2), and dashboard updating (4.3)—so split it only where each resulting question retains at least two values, or move values to existing dimensions whose questions they answer. Dimension 6 combines authentication (6.1), logout/session termination (6.2–6.3), and a generic security claim (6.4); reorganize these into existing access/security decision points while preserving at least two candidates per point. Dimension 10 mixes encryption mode (10.1–10.2), data scope (10.3), transmission handling (10.4), and credential storage (10.5); split or move these values so each dimension represents one question with at least two candidates. Dimension 11 also mixes report assembly, report-format variation, and the outcome of downloadable reports (11.2), requiring reorganization around the actual decision questions.

The main overlap is between Bike Status Dissemination (3) and Monitoring Data Presentation (5): dashboard and monitoring updates in 3.1 are equally valid answers to 5, so move the monitoring/dashboard portion to 5 while retaining rider-status dissemination in 3. criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions and values are labeled distinctly: payment-provider adaptation in 9.2, the 1000-meter-style proximity query in 4.2, and in-transit versus at-rest protection in 10.1 and 10.2 are understandable. However, dimension 1, "Rental Lifecycle and Behavior," combines lifecycle, command encapsulation, event automation, and pricing; reorganize its existing values into narrower dimensions or drop the isolated pricing value 1.4. Value 7.4, "Secure user access control," is a vague security objective rather than a distinguishable session-termination choice; drop it or replace it by reorganizing existing session-policy content. Value 10.7, "Biometric privacy protection," is similarly an undifferentiated objective overlapping the concrete deletion mechanism 10.6; drop 10.7. Value 12.5, "Registration data security considerations," is a broad summary that overlaps values 12.1–12.4 rather than a distinct registration-data scope alternative; drop it. Dimension 5's values 5.1 and 5.2 are understandable, but its name and description should explicitly distinguish data aggregation from update delivery so the two existing values are not read as interchangeable.

Reorganize existing dimensions and values so 3 explicitly distinguishes communication alternatives and 10 explicitly distinguishes compliance mechanisms; the missing infrastructure and observability concerns cannot be represented by the current dimensions without adding content.
